content.thinking:
I need to write this postmortem without inventing specific figures, using placeholders instead. The key fact is that metrics stopped arriving while the service itself kept running fine for shoppers—so monitoring went blind without any real customer impact. I'm starting the causal chain with that initial symptom: metrics missing while the underlying service remained healthy.

For step two, the deploy that renamed the scrape port looks like the trigger, but that specific detail about the port rename comes from the investigator's hypothesis rather than a directly verified record—so I should present the timing correlation (metrics stopping right before the deploy, then rollback restoring visibility) as solid evidence, while treating the exact mechanism as an assumption that needs hedging even though it's been marked confirmed.

For contributing factors, I'm planning new action items: a CI check to verify the scrape port config matches between deploy and monitoring setup, and a synthetic health probe so the team can judge service health independently when metrics go absent rather than relying solely on rollback as a fix.

Thinking through lessons: the team got lucky since the service wasn't actually failing during the blind monitoring period, so if it had failed simultaneously nobody would have noticed. What went well was that Argus checked logs directly to confirm the service was healthy, and the rollback decision was confirmed quickly. What went wrong was the monitoring blind spot itself and the delay before the alert fired after the incident actually began.

I also need to flag that the rollback reverts the whole deploy revision, which could unintentionally drop other unrelated changes bundled in that same deploy. For the writeup I should avoid citing specific numeric durations or digits, keeping language qualitative like "for at least" without exact figures, though "labels" as a term is fine to use. For the error rate during the broken window, I'll point to the log signals rather than metrics since metrics were absent then, referencing the relevant log entries as the supporting evidence.

action_items.item: Add a CI or deploy-time check that renders io-shop's production values and fails if the metrics port name does not match the name the scrape target or service monitor selects.
Add an external black-box probe of the shop's account page, with its own alert, so shopper health can be judged when the metrics series is absent.

Name an owner for the port-name contract between service configuration and monitoring. Re-land the intended port rename only together with the matching scraper change, and confirm samples arrive after the deploy.

causal_chain.step: Metrics from io-shop stopped arriving, so the MetricsAbsent alert fired at {alert_raised}. The last sample was at {T5.2}. Meanwhile the shop did not visibly fail: its error rate was {errors_while_broken} while broken against {errors_before} before, and the logs show only the usual ClientDisconnected errors.

The metrics series ended immediately before a production deploy. Revision 9f4ad14582c99c497eb6c2d2af87566cd4493020 went out at {P1.1}, and the first missing minute is {began}. No flag changes were recorded, so the deploy was the only change in that window.

Rolling the deploy back made the service readable again. This confirms the deploy's configuration, and not the application's traffic handling, broke metrics collection. The Investigator's account is that the deploy renamed the scrape port to 'http-metrics', so the scrape target no longer matched. The record does not show the rename directly.

The deploy reached production with nothing checking that the scrape or monitor configuration still matched the service's configuration. The Code-Fix Agent found no code to change, which fits a configuration-only fault.

contributing_factors.factor: No pre-deploy or post-deploy check that the metrics port name in io-shop's values still matches what the scraper selects. A configuration rename could silently cut off monitoring.

Detection relied entirely on the metrics pipeline. When it went blind, nothing independent showed whether shoppers were affected, and the alert fired {alert_raised - began} after onset. The only health evidence was the logs.

The rollback undid the whole revision to fix a monitoring-only fault. Nobody owns the port-name contract between the service configuration and the scraper, so the rename could be re-attempted and break again.

input.executive_summary: Monitoring lost sight of the shop. Metrics from io-shop stopped arriving at {began}, right after a deploy, and an alert for the missing data fired at {alert_raised}. The shop itself appears to have kept working. Its error rate while the metrics were missing was {errors_while_broken}, against {errors_before} before, and the logs show only routine errors. The data gap lasted at least {duration}, which is a lower bound. Argus rolled the deploy back, and by {closed} the service could be read again. Shoppers were apparently not affected. The gap was in the team's ability to see whether the shop was healthy.

got_lucky: The shop was healthy during the blind period. A real failure at the same time would have gone unseen by metrics for at least {duration}.
went_well: Argus read the logs alongside the missing metrics and saw that the shop was still serving normally, so the incident was not treated as a shopper outage.
The leading candidate pointed at the single deploy in the window, and the rollback restored readable metrics within {held} of the incident being picked up.
went_wrong: A configuration change cut off monitoring and nothing caught it before or at deploy time.
The alert only said that samples were missing, so health during the gap had to be inferred from sparse log lines.
The fix was a full rollback, which also reverts anything else in that revision, rather than a targeted correction of the port name.

input.root_cause: The deploy of revision 9f4ad14582c99c497eb6c2d2af87566cd4493020 at {P1.1} changed io-shop's production configuration, which the Investigator's account traces to a rename of the metrics port from 'metrics' to 'http-metrics'. Nothing checked that the monitoring side still matched. Metrics collection from io-shop stopped while the shop kept serving, and rolling the deploy back made the service readable again.
input.symptom: Shop metrics stopped arriving; shoppers apparently unaffected
